meta.name: Cisco Certified DevNet Associate (DEVASC 200-901)
meta.notes: Initial DevNet Associate pack — covers REST status semantics, OAuth 2.0, NETCONF/YANG/RESTCONF, Git workflows, Meraki Dashboard API pagination, DNA Center vs vManage scope, Docker image vs container, webhooks vs polling, 12-factor config, Ansible idempotency, Webex bot tokens, and ACI APIC policy model. Answer positions balanced 3/3/3/3 across A/B/C/D. v1.1: +10 — 429/Retry-After, 401 vs 403, RESTCONF vs NETCONF, secrets handling, CI definition, YAML recognition, DevNet Sandbox, /28 subnetting, raise_for_status, git clone.

questions.question: A developer issues a POST to `/api/v1/devices` and the server creates the new device record. According to REST conventions, which HTTP status code should the API return, and what header is typically included?
options: 200 OK with a `Content-Length` header pointing at the new resource
201 Created with a `Location` header pointing at the new resource URI
202 Accepted with a `Retry-After` header for polling
204 No Content with an empty response body and no headers
questions.explanation: When a POST successfully creates a resource the standard response is 201 Created together with a `Location` header that contains the URI of the newly-created resource. 200 OK is used for successful GET/PUT that returns a body, 202 Accepted means the request was queued for asynchronous processing, and 204 No Content means success with deliberately no body (typical for DELETE).

questions.question: You are integrating a third-party application with the Webex REST API on behalf of end users. The application must let each user grant scoped, revocable access without exposing their Webex password. Which authentication mechanism is the correct fit?
options: HTTP Basic authentication with the user's Webex email and password
A long-lived static API key embedded in the application binary
Mutual TLS using the application's X.509 client certificate
OAuth 2.0 Authorization Code grant returning a short-lived access token
questions.explanation: OAuth 2.0 with the Authorization Code grant is designed exactly for this: the user authenticates directly with Webex, consents to specific scopes, and the app receives a short-lived access token (plus refresh token) without ever seeing the password. Basic auth exposes credentials, a static embedded key is not per-user and cannot be revoked granularly, and mTLS authenticates the app itself rather than a delegated user.

questions.question: A network engineer wants to programmatically configure an IOS XE device using a YANG-defined data model over a session-oriented, transactional protocol that supports candidate configurations and `commit`/`rollback`. Which protocol meets these requirements?
options: NETCONF over SSH on TCP/830
RESTCONF over HTTPS on TCP/443
gNMI over HTTP/2 on TCP/9339
SNMPv3 over UDP/161 with SET PDUs
questions.explanation: NETCONF runs over SSH on TCP/830, maintains a persistent session, and supports the `<candidate>` datastore with `<commit>` and `<discard-changes>`/rollback — true transactional configuration. RESTCONF is stateless HTTP and exposes YANG data per-request without a candidate-store transaction. gNMI is Google's streaming-telemetry/configuration protocol but does not use the NETCONF candidate/commit model. SNMP has no YANG or transactional semantics.

questions.question: Two developers have been working on parallel feature branches. Before merging into `main`, the team lead wants the feature history to appear as a single linear sequence of commits on top of the latest `main` — without any merge-commit bubbles. Which Git operation should each developer run on their feature branch first?
options: `git merge main` to fast-forward main into the feature branch
`git cherry-pick main` to copy main's commits onto the feature branch
`git rebase main` to replay the feature commits on top of main
`git reset --hard main` to align the branch with main
questions.explanation: `git rebase main` rewrites the feature branch so its commits are replayed on top of the current `main`, producing a linear history with no merge commits when the branch is finally fast-forwarded in. `git merge main` would create exactly the merge-commit bubble the lead wants to avoid. `git cherry-pick` copies individual commits, not a branch, and is the wrong tool here. `git reset --hard main` would destroy the feature work entirely.

questions.question: A script that pulls clients from the Meraki Dashboard API receives an HTTP 200 with a `Link` header containing `rel="next"`. What does this indicate and what should the script do?
options: The API is rate-limited; the script must back off using the Retry-After value
The response is paginated; the script should follow the `next` URL to retrieve the remaining records
The organization has been migrated; the script should re-authenticate against the new region
A schema change has occurred; the script should fetch the OpenAPI spec from the `next` link
questions.explanation: The Meraki Dashboard API paginates large result sets and returns RFC 5988 `Link` headers with `rel="first"`, `rel="prev"`, `rel="next"`, `rel="last"`. A `rel="next"` link means more pages exist and the client should issue a GET against that URL to continue. Rate-limit signalling uses 429 with `Retry-After`, region migrations are signalled with 3xx redirects to a regional base URL, and schema discovery is unrelated to pagination headers.

questions.question: Your team needs a single controller that provides intent-based, automated provisioning, assurance and segmentation for an enterprise **campus and branch LAN/Wi-Fi** fabric. Which Cisco platform is purpose-built for this scope?
options: Cisco DNA Center (now Catalyst Center)
Cisco vManage (Catalyst SD-WAN Manager)
Cisco APIC (Application Policy Infrastructure Controller)
Cisco Intersight
questions.explanation: Cisco DNA Center / Catalyst Center is the intent-based controller for enterprise campus and branch LAN/Wi-Fi (SD-Access fabric, assurance, automated provisioning). vManage is the controller for SD-WAN (WAN overlays between sites), not LAN/Wi-Fi. APIC is the controller for the ACI data-center fabric. Intersight is for compute/UCS and HyperFlex infrastructure lifecycle.

questions.question: A developer runs `docker build -t myapp:1.0 .` followed by `docker run -d myapp:1.0`. Which statement most accurately describes the relationship between the two artifacts produced?
options: The image is a running instance; the container is the immutable read-only template
Image and container are interchangeable terms; Docker uses them as synonyms
The container is the build cache; the image is the running process namespace
The image is an immutable, layered read-only template; the container is a running, writable instance of that image
questions.explanation: A Docker image is built once from a Dockerfile and is an immutable, layered, read-only template. `docker run` instantiates a container from that image by adding a thin writable layer on top and starting the entry-point process inside isolated namespaces. The other options invert or conflate the two concepts.

questions.question: An app currently polls a Webex REST endpoint every 5 seconds to learn when new messages are posted in a room. Traffic and quota usage are excessive. Which mechanism would let Webex notify the app only when a relevant event actually occurs?
options: Increase the polling interval to 60 seconds and add exponential backoff
Register a Webex webhook with a public HTTPS callback URL filtered by room and resource
Open an SSH tunnel to the Webex API and read events from its standard output
Use SNMP traps from the Webex cloud to the application
questions.explanation: Webhooks invert the polling pattern: the app registers an HTTPS callback URL plus a resource/event filter (e.g. `messages`/`created` for a specific room), and Webex POSTs an event payload to that URL only when the event fires — eliminating most quota usage. Slower polling is still polling. SSH tunnelling is not a Webex API pattern, and SNMP is a network-management protocol unrelated to Webex collaboration APIs.

questions.question: While reviewing a containerised microservice against the Twelve-Factor App methodology, you notice the database password is hard-coded into a `config.py` file checked into Git. Which factor does this violate, and what is the recommended remediation?
options: Factor I (Codebase) — split the repository into one repo per environment
Factor VI (Processes) — make the process stateful so credentials persist in memory
Factor III (Config) — store config (including secrets) in environment variables, not in code
Factor X (Dev/prod parity) — ensure prod and dev share the same hard-coded credentials
questions.explanation: Twelve-Factor Factor III, Config, says strict separation of config from code: anything that varies between deploys (credentials, host names, endpoints) belongs in environment variables, not in source. Factor I argues for one codebase tracked in revision control with many deploys (not per-env repos). Factor VI explicitly requires processes to be stateless. Factor X is about keeping environments as similar as possible — never by sharing the same hard-coded secret.

questions.question: An Ansible playbook with the task `ios_config: lines: ['ntp server 10.0.0.1']` is run twice against the same router. After the second run the change report shows `changed=0`. Which Ansible property explains this behaviour?
options: Eventual consistency — Ansible needs a third run to converge
Push-mode delivery — the second run was silently dropped by the SSH transport
Stateless execution — Ansible always reports `changed=0` after the first run
Idempotency — modules check current state and only apply changes when actual state differs from declared state
questions.explanation: Ansible modules are designed to be idempotent: `ios_config` reads the running configuration, compares it against the declared `lines`, and only pushes a change if the line is missing. Re-running a converged playbook therefore reports `changed=0`. The other options describe behaviours that Ansible does not have: there is no eventual-consistency lag, runs are not silently dropped, and `changed=0` is the result of a state check, not a stateless default.

questions.question: You are building a Webex chatbot that must reply in any space it is added to. Which credential should the bot use to authenticate to the Webex REST API, and what is its key security property?
options: A Bot access token issued when the bot is created on developer.webex.com — it is scoped to the bot account and only sees messages addressed to it in group spaces
The developer's personal access token — it inherits the developer's full user permissions and never expires
A guest-issuer JWT signed with the organisation's shared secret — it grants admin-equivalent access to every space
An OAuth client secret used directly as a bearer token in the Authorization header
questions.explanation: Bots authenticate with a dedicated Bot access token generated when the bot is registered on developer.webex.com. It identifies the bot as its own user, and in group spaces the bot only receives messages where it is explicitly @-mentioned — an important privacy property. A personal access token is for development only and tied to a human identity. Guest-issuer tokens are for embedding guest users (not bots) and are not admin-level. OAuth client secrets are used to *obtain* tokens, not as bearer tokens themselves.

questions.question: In a Cisco ACI fabric, which controller exposes the northbound REST API that developers use to define tenants, application profiles, EPGs and contracts as JSON or XML objects in the Management Information Tree?
options: Cisco DNA Center (Catalyst Center)
Cisco vManage (Catalyst SD-WAN Manager)
Cisco APIC (Application Policy Infrastructure Controller)
Cisco Intersight
questions.explanation: APIC is the centralised policy controller for an ACI data-center fabric and exposes the REST API used to read and write objects in the Management Information Tree (MIT) — tenants, application profiles, EPGs, contracts, bridge domains, etc. DNA Center / Catalyst Center is the controller for campus/branch SD-Access, vManage is the controller for SD-WAN, and Intersight manages UCS/HyperFlex compute infrastructure.

questions.question: A script calling a REST API suddenly receives HTTP 429 responses with a `Retry-After: 30` header. What is the API telling the client?
options: The request body failed schema validation and must be corrected before resending it
The endpoint has moved permanently and requests should be redirected to a new URL
The client has exceeded the rate limit and should wait 30 seconds before retrying
The server is permanently rejecting this client and the API key must be regenerated
questions.explanation: 429 Too Many Requests is the rate-limiting status code, and Retry-After tells the client how long to back off. Schema validation failures return 400, permanent moves return 301, and a revoked credential would produce 401/403 — none of which carry the back-off semantics of 429. Well-behaved API clients honor Retry-After or apply exponential backoff.

questions.question: A request with a valid, unexpired token returns HTTP 403 from one endpoint while other endpoints return 200. What does the 403 indicate?
options: The token could not be authenticated, so the client must log in again to obtain a new one
The client is authenticated but not authorized to perform this action on this resource
The endpoint exists but the resource it would return has been deleted from the server
The TLS handshake failed, so the request never actually reached the application layer
questions.explanation: 403 Forbidden means the server knows who you are and refuses the action anyway — an authorization (permissions/scope) failure. 401 Unauthorized is the authentication failure that calls for new credentials; a deleted resource yields 404 (or 410); a failed TLS handshake never produces an HTTP status at all. The 401-vs-403 distinction is a DEVASC staple.

questions.question: Which statement correctly contrasts RESTCONF with NETCONF?
options: RESTCONF uses HTTP(S) with JSON or XML encodings, while NETCONF runs over SSH using XML and RPCs
RESTCONF can only read operational data, while NETCONF is required for any configuration change
RESTCONF uses proprietary Cisco data models, while NETCONF works exclusively with OpenConfig models
RESTCONF maintains a long-lived stateful session, while NETCONF is entirely stateless per request
questions.explanation: Both protocols drive the same YANG data models, but the transports differ: RESTCONF is a stateless HTTP(S) interface using JSON or XML, while NETCONF runs RPCs over an SSH session and supports features like candidate datastores and locks. Both can read and write configuration; both use standard or vendor YANG models — the model layer is independent of the protocol.

questions.question: A reviewer rejects a pull request because the script contains `API_KEY = "a91xZ…"` directly in the source. What is the recommended remediation?
options: Move the key into a code comment so it is ignored by the interpreter at runtime
Base64-encode the key in place so it is no longer human-readable anywhere in the repository history
Split the key across two variables so automated secret scanners no longer detect it
Read the key from an environment variable or secrets manager instead of the source code
questions.explanation: Secrets do not belong in source control: inject them at runtime from environment variables or a secrets manager, and rotate the exposed key since git history already contains it. Comments still ship in the repo; Base64 is encoding, not encryption; splitting a secret to defeat scanners hides the problem instead of fixing it.

questions.question: In a CI/CD pipeline, what characterizes the CONTINUOUS INTEGRATION stage specifically?
options: Production traffic is shifted gradually to the new version of the service while error rates and latency are monitored
Infrastructure capacity is scaled ahead of an expected release-day traffic increase
Every commit triggers an automated build and the test suite, so integration problems surface immediately
Completed releases are deployed automatically to production with no human approval step
questions.explanation: CI is the practice of merging changes frequently with each commit automatically built and tested, catching integration breakage within minutes of its introduction. Automatic production deployment describes continuous deployment; gradual traffic shifting is a canary/progressive delivery technique; capacity planning is operations work outside the CI definition.

questions.question: Which snippet is valid YAML for a list of two interfaces, each with a name and a description?
options:
interfaces:
  - name: Gi0/0
    description: uplink
  - name: Gi0/1
    description: access
<interfaces><name>Gi0/0</name><description>uplink</description></interfaces>
interfaces = [{name: Gi0/0, description: uplink}, {name: Gi0/1, description: access-port}];  // config
{ "interfaces": [ "name": "Gi0/0", "description": "uplink" ] }
questions.explanation: YAML expresses lists with `-` items and nesting with indentation — the first snippet is a list of two mappings under the `interfaces` key. The second is XML, the third is a programming-language assignment statement, and the fourth is malformed JSON (an array cannot directly contain key-value pairs). Recognising data formats on sight is an explicit DEVASC exam objective.

questions.question: A developer wants to test scripts against a real Cisco DNA Center and IOS XE devices but has no lab hardware and must not touch the production network. What does Cisco provide for exactly this purpose?
options: The DevNet Sandbox — free, reservable hosted lab environments for Cisco platforms and APIs
A read-write demonstration tenant inside every customer's production DNA Center license
The Cisco TAC remote-access program, which lends partner engineers supervised time on customer systems
Packet Tracer, which fully emulates DNA Center REST APIs for automated testing
questions.explanation: DevNet Sandboxes are Cisco-hosted, free environments — always-on or reservable — running real platforms (DNA Center, IOS XE on CML, Meraki, Webex and more) for development and testing without production risk. There is no demo tenant baked into customer licenses; TAC handles support cases, not lab access; Packet Tracer simulates networks for learning but does not expose DNA Center's APIs.

questions.question: How many usable host addresses does the subnet 192.168.10.0/28 provide?
questions.explanation: A /28 leaves 4 host bits → 2⁴ = 16 total addresses, minus the network and broadcast addresses = 14 usable hosts. 16 forgets to subtract the two reserved addresses; 30 and 62 correspond to /27 and /26 respectively — classic off-by-one-prefix distractors.

questions.question: A Python script must stop with a clear error when an API call fails, instead of crashing later while parsing the body. Given `response = requests.get(url)`, which line implements this idiomatically?
options: if response.text == 'error': sys.exit(1)
assert response.json() is not None
response.raise_for_status()
while response.status_code != 200: response = requests.get(url)
questions.explanation: `raise_for_status()` raises an HTTPError for any 4xx/5xx response, failing fast at the call site with the status code in the exception. Comparing body text to 'error' is fragile; asserting on `.json()` crashes on non-JSON error bodies — the original problem; the while-loop retries forever on persistent failures and hammers the API.

questions.question: A teammate asks you to copy a repository from GitHub to your laptop so you can work on a feature branch locally. Which command does this?
options: git checkout https://github.com/org/repo.git
git fork https://github.com/org/repo.git
git pull https://github.com/org/repo.git
git clone https://github.com/org/repo.git
questions.explanation: `git clone` copies a remote repository — full history, branches and remote configuration — to the local machine. `checkout` switches branches or restores files in an existing repo; forking is a server-side platform action, not a git command; `pull` fetches and merges into a repository you already have, and cannot create one.
